lessons.0.slides.0.title: DRC: A Legend of the Wine World
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 20 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: An in-depth look at the birthplace of the world's most expensive wines
lessons.0.slides.1.title: DRC's Historical Legacy
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti was formally established in 1869, but its history traces back to the 13th century. The Romanée-Conti parcel was purchased in 1760 by the Prince de Conti, who outbid Madame de Pompadour, Louis XV's mistress, to acquire it — and renamed it after himself. It is now jointly owned by the de Villaine and Leroy-Roch families.

lessons.0.slides.4.content: Area ranges from 1.8ha (RC) to 6.06ha (La Tâche), but price is inversely correlated. RC's smallest area commands the highest price, proving that rarity determines value.
lessons.0.slides.5.title: DRC's Winemaking Philosophy
lessons.0.slides.5.content: DRC converted fully to biodynamic farming in 1985, making it one of the earliest practitioners among Burgundy's top domaines. They believe only healthy soil can produce great wine. Winemaking includes 100% whole-cluster fermentation, 100% new oak barrels, no filtration, no fining — pursuing pure terroir expression.

lessons.0.slides.6.points.0: Ultra-low yields: only 20–25 hl/ha, well below the legal maximum
lessons.0.slides.6.points.1: 100% whole-cluster fermentation: stems retained for complexity
lessons.0.slides.6.points.2: 100% new oak barrels: sourced from the estate's own Allier forest
lessons.0.slides.6.points.3: Extended ageing: minimum 18 months in barrel
lessons.0.slides.6.points.4: No filtration, no fining: preserving all terroir information
lessons.0.slides.6.points.5: Delayed bottling: 6–12 months later than typical domaines

lessons.0.slides.7.rightPoints.2: Style: perfect balance of power and elegance
lessons.0.slides.8.title: Why Is DRC So Expensive?
lessons.0.slides.8.content: DRC's extraordinary prices stem from multiple factors: 1) extreme rarity (Romanée-Conti is just 1.8 hectares); 2) unrivalled quality consistency; 3) centuries of prestige; 4) the high cost of biodynamic farming; 5) demand that vastly exceeds supply. A single bottle of Romanée-Conti costs as much as a car — and prices keep rising.

lessons.1.title: Domaine Leroy
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Domaine Leroy: Biodynamics at its Pinnacle
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 18 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: How Lalou Bize-Leroy built one of Burgundy's most expensive and philosophically rigorous domaines
lessons.1.slides.1.title: The Iron Lady: Lalou Bize-Leroy
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Lalou Bize-Leroy is arguably the most influential living figure in Burgundy. Born in 1932, she co-directed DRC for decades before founding Domaine Leroy in 1988 by purchasing Domaine Charles Noellat. Her biodynamic philosophy and perfectionist standards have made Domaine Leroy wines among the most expensive in the world.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🌿 Leroy's Biodynamic Practice
lessons.1.slides.2.points.0: Homeopathic yields: 10–15 hl/ha — among the lowest in all of Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.2.points.1: No synthetic chemicals ever — certified biodynamic since 1988
lessons.1.slides.2.points.2: Biodynamic preparations 500, 501, 502–508 applied on precise lunar calendar
lessons.1.slides.2.points.3: Manual harvest only, multiple passes through the vineyard
lessons.1.slides.2.points.4: Grapes harvested in small baskets — no crushing before the cellar
lessons.1.slides.2.points.5: Zero new oak: old barrels (3–5 years) to avoid masking terroir

lessons.1.slides.4.title: 🧪 Biodynamic Preparations Explained
lessons.1.slides.4.points.0: Preparation 500 (Horn Manure): cow manure fermented in cow horn underground over winter — stimulates soil microbial life
lessons.1.slides.4.points.1: Preparation 501 (Horn Silica): ground quartz in cow horn, buried in summer — enhances photosynthesis and fruit ripening
lessons.1.slides.4.points.2: Preparations 502–508 (Compost Preparations): plant-based (yarrow, chamomile, valerian etc.) — regulate compost decomposition
lessons.1.slides.4.points.3: Spraying follows lunar calendar: root days (best for pruning), flower days (best for tasting), fruit days (harvest)
lessons.1.slides.5.title: Domaine Leroy's Grand Cru Portfolio
lessons.1.slides.5.content: In 1988, Lalou acquired Domaine Charles Noellat's extensive portfolio including multiple Grand Cru parcels across the Côte de Nuits. Combined with her personal holdings (Domaine d'Auvenay), she controls some of the finest terroir in Burgundy — farmed to extreme standards and produced in tiny quantities.
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 🍷 Leroy's Key Grand Crus
lessons.1.slides.6.points.0: Musigny (0.27ha) — possibly Burgundy's most sought-after Leroy wine
lessons.1.slides.6.points.4: Clos de Vougeot (1.91ha) — textbook expression of the climat
lessons.1.slides.7.title: Domaine Leroy vs Maison Leroy
lessons.1.slides.7.rightPoints.3: Includes aged Burgundy stock from all eras
lessons.1.slides.7.rightPoints.4: Prices: wide range, from village to historic
lessons.1.slides.8.title: Leroy Style: Concentration and Elegance United
lessons.1.slides.8.content: Unlike the power-elegance trade-off seen in many great producers, Leroy wines achieve both simultaneously. The ultra-low yields produce extraordinary concentration; the old-oak, minimal-intervention approach preserves freshness and definition. Critics describe Leroy's top wines as having 'impossible density with impossible lightness.'

lessons.2.title: Domaine Armand Rousseau
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Armand Rousseau: King of Gevrey
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 15 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: The reference producer for Gevrey-Chambertin and the Chambertin Grand Cru
lessons.2.slides.1.title: The Synonym for Gevrey-Chambertin
lessons.2.slides.1.content: If one name defines Gevrey-Chambertin, it is Armand Rousseau. Founded in the 1930s, the domaine has been run by Charles Rousseau (son of Armand) and his son Eric since 2012. Their holdings encompass the finest parcels of Chambertin, Clos de Bèze, Clos Saint-Jacques and several other Premiers and Grands Crus.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 👑 Rousseau's Premier Portfolio
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: Chambertin (1.4ha) — Napoleonic history, the most 'complete' Burgundy
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: Chambertin Clos de Bèze (1.42ha) — arguably more consistent than Chambertin
lessons.2.slides.2.points.2: Clos Saint-Jacques (2.18ha) — premier cru that performs like Grand Cru
lessons.2.slides.2.points.3: Gevrey-Chambertin Cazetiers — one of Gevrey's finest premier parcels
lessons.2.slides.3.title: Rousseau's Winemaking Philosophy
lessons.2.slides.3.content: Rousseau practices what might be called 'transparent traditionalism' — traditional methods applied with scientific precision. They use partial whole-cluster (10–30% depending on vintage), age in 30–50% new oak, and never filter. The goal is wines that express Gevrey's power and iron character while retaining elegance.
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 🍇 Rousseau's Winemaking Profile
lessons.2.slides.4.points.3: 30–50% new oak: more restrained than historical Gevrey style
lessons.2.slides.5.title: Chambertin vs Clos de Bèze
lessons.2.slides.5.leftPoints.2: Style: maximum structure, iron, dark fruit
lessons.2.slides.5.rightPoints.1: Pre-dates Chambertin — established by Bèze abbey 640 AD
lessons.2.slides.5.rightPoints.2: Style: slightly more refined, immediately expressive

lessons.2.slides.6.title: Clos Saint-Jacques: The Best Premier Cru?
lessons.2.slides.6.content: Rousseau's Clos Saint-Jacques is frequently cited as evidence that Premier Cru classification can be misleading. Priced and performing at Grand Cru level, this 6.7-hectare walled vineyard sits immediately above the village of Gevrey on a north-facing slope — unusual for such quality. Rousseau owns 2.18 hectares and consistently produces one of Burgundy's most sought-after wines.

lessons.3.title: Domaine Coche-Dury (The White Wine King)
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Coche-Dury: The Ultimate White Wine Standard
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 15 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: The most difficult Burgundy white wines to buy — and why they set the global standard
lessons.3.slides.1.title: The Most Impossible Burgundy White to Buy
lessons.3.slides.1.content: Domaine Coche-Dury in Meursault produces, by near-universal consensus, the finest white wines in Burgundy and arguably the world. Founded by Jean-François Coche (now run by son Raphaël), the domaine's Meursault Perrières and Corton-Charlemagne are the stuff of legend — allocated to a tiny list of privileged buyers and virtually impossible to purchase at retail.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🌟 Coche-Dury's Premier Whites
lessons.3.slides.2.points.0: Corton-Charlemagne (0.34ha) — $1,500–3,000/bottle; arguably the best expression of this Grand Cru
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: Meursault Les Perrières (0.41ha) — $800–1,500/bottle; Coche's signature wine
lessons.3.slides.2.points.2: Meursault Les Rougeots — $400–700; outstanding village Meursault
lessons.3.slides.2.points.3: Puligny-Montrachet (0.15ha) — rare even by Coche standards
lessons.3.slides.3.title: Coche-Dury's Winemaking Secrets
lessons.3.slides.3.content: Coche-Dury's methods are deceptively simple: old vines (40–60+ years), extremely low yields (25–35 hl/ha), whole-cluster pressing, ageing on full lees with bâtonnage for 12–18 months, and minimal new oak (20–30%). The complexity emerges not from technique but from vineyard quality and absolute non-intervention.
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 🔬 Coche-Dury: Winemaking Details
lessons.3.slides.4.points.0: Old vines: 40–60+ years — deep roots, complex flavour
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: Full lees ageing: 12–18 months with bâtonnage (lees stirring)
lessons.3.slides.4.points.4: Minimal new oak: 20–30% for villages; 0–15% for Perrières
lessons.3.slides.4.points.5: No fining, minimal filtration, hand bottling by gravity
lessons.3.slides.5.title: Meursault Les Perrières: The Legend
lessons.3.slides.5.content: Meursault Les Perrières is the finest Premier Cru in Meursault and regularly outperforms many Grands Crus in blind tastings. Its position — steep, rocky, Kimmeridgian limestone — produces wines of razor precision, stony minerality and extraordinary longevity. In Coche-Dury's hands, Perrières represents the pinnacle of Meursault expression.

lessons.4.title: Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé
lessons.4.slides.0.title: Comte de Vogüé: Guardian of Musigny
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 15 minutes
lessons.4.slides.0.description: The largest owner in Musigny — and the domaine's remarkable quality renaissance since the 1990s
lessons.4.slides.1.title: Musigny's Largest Landowner
lessons.4.slides.1.content: Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé owns 7.2 of Musigny's 10.85 hectares — making it by far the parcel's dominant owner. Along with Bonnes-Mares and Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses, Vogüé controls the finest terroir in Chambolle-Musigny. However, the domaine experienced a difficult period in the 1970s–1980s, from which it emerged triumphantly in the 1990s under winemaker François Millet.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: 🏰 Vogüé's Core Holdings
lessons.4.slides.2.points.0: Musigny (7.2ha of 10.85ha total) — dominant owner; the most perfumed Grand Cru
lessons.4.slides.2.points.1: Bonnes-Mares (2.7ha) — power counterpoint to Musigny's delicacy
lessons.4.slides.2.points.2: Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses (0.57ha) — finest Premier Cru in village
lessons.4.slides.2.points.4: Bourgogne Blanc — Chardonnay from young Musigny vines
lessons.4.slides.3.title: The 1990s Renaissance
lessons.4.slides.3.content: After years of disappointing wines in the 1970s and early 1980s — widely attributed to excessive yields and vine selection issues — Vogüé's fortunes transformed when François Millet joined as winemaker in 1986. A systematic replanting programme, reduced yields, and improved cellar practice restored Vogüé to the Burgundy elite by the mid-1990s.

lessons.4.slides.4.points.0: Systematic replanting from late 1980s — replacing old, virus-infected vines with healthy material
lessons.4.slides.4.points.1: Yield reduction: from 50+ hl/ha to 30–35 hl/ha through green harvesting
lessons.4.slides.4.points.2: Whole-cluster percentage increased: 20–40% depending on vintage
lessons.4.slides.4.points.3: Oak regime reformed: 40–60% new oak; quality barrels from top coopers
lessons.4.slides.4.points.4: Musigny Blanc production suspended 1994–2014: young vines declassified to Bourgogne Blanc
lessons.4.slides.4.points.5: François Millet's 30-year tenure: consistent improvement across all wines

lessons.4.slides.6.title: Musigny Blanc: The Ultra-Rare White
lessons.4.slides.6.content: Vogüé's Musigny Blanc is among the rarest white Burgundies in existence. The Musigny Grand Cru appellation theoretically permits both red and white wine, but only Vogüé produces white — from a tiny Chardonnay parcel. From 1994 to 2014, young vine replanting meant all Musigny Blanc was declassified to Bourgogne Blanc. The return to Musigny Blanc in 2014 was a major Burgundy event.

lessons.5.slides.0.title: The New Generation's Rise
lessons.5.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 6 - 15 minutes
lessons.5.slides.0.description: How outsiders and métayage farmers became Burgundy legends — and Henri Jayer's lasting legacy
lessons.5.slides.1.title: Domaine Dujac: Pioneer of Whole-Cluster Fermentation
lessons.5.slides.1.content: Domaine Dujac was founded in 1967 by Jacques Seysses — an outsider from Paris who had no family wine background. Through study, passion and an extraordinary eye for buying undervalued Grand Cru parcels, Seysses built one of Burgundy's finest domaines. Dujac is famous for its high whole-cluster percentage, which produces wines of remarkable perfume and suppleness.
lessons.5.slides.2.title: 🌟 Dujac's Core Holdings
lessons.5.slides.2.points.0: Clos Saint-Denis (1.48ha) — Dujac's signature Grand Cru; perfumed, complex
lessons.5.slides.2.points.1: Clos de la Roche (0.72ha) — the most powerful Dujac Grand Cru
lessons.5.slides.3.title: Domaine Méo-Camuzet: The Métayage Master
lessons.5.slides.3.content: Domaine Méo-Camuzet's story is one of Burgundy's most remarkable transformations. Jean-Nicolas Méo inherited a large portfolio of Grand Cru parcels from his great-uncle Etienne Camuzet — but they were farmed by tenant farmers (métayers) including Henri Jayer. When Jayer retired in 1988, Méo took back direct control and, with Jayer's guidance, built one of Burgundy's top domaines within a decade.

lessons.5.slides.4.points.1: Clos de Vougeot (3.03ha) — large holding across multiple positions
lessons.5.slides.5.title: Dujac vs Méo-Camuzet
lessons.5.slides.6.title: Henri Jayer's Legacy
lessons.5.slides.6.content: Henri Jayer (1922–2006) is widely considered the greatest vigneron of the 20th century. His approach — destemming, cold pre-fermentation maceration, new oak ageing — became the template for modern Burgundy. His wines (especially Vosne-Romanée Cros Parantoux) regularly sell for $10,000–50,000 per bottle at auction. Jayer influenced virtually every great winemaker in Burgundy through his mentorship.

lessons.5.slides.8.title: 🎓 Henri Jayer's Core Winemaking Philosophy
lessons.5.slides.8.points.0: Total destemming: no whole clusters — stems contain harsh tannins
lessons.5.slides.8.points.1: Cold pre-fermentation maceration: 6–8 days at 12–14°C to extract colour/aroma without alcohol
lessons.5.slides.8.points.2: Short fermentation: 8–12 days with gentle pigeage (punch-down)
lessons.5.slides.8.points.3: 100% new oak: each vintage in brand new barrels
lessons.5.slides.8.points.4: No fining, no filtration: 'the wine knows best'
lessons.5.slides.8.points.5: Low yields: rigorous green harvesting; 25–30 hl/ha
lessons.5.slides.9.title: Métayage (Sharecropping) System Evolution
lessons.5.slides.9.leftPoints.0: Landowner provides land, tenant provides labour
lessons.5.slides.9.leftPoints.1: Harvest split 50/50 between landowner and tenant
lessons.5.slides.9.leftPoints.3: Enabled Jayer to build reputation with others' land
lessons.5.slides.9.leftPoints.4: Landowner often sold their share as bulk wine
lessons.5.slides.9.rightPoints.0: Landowners increasingly take back direct control
lessons.5.slides.9.rightPoints.4: Méo-Camuzet's takeover from Jayer is the defining example

lessons.6.slides.0.title: Master Producer Style Comparison
lessons.6.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 7 - 15 minutes
lessons.6.slides.0.description: Synthesising the stylistic differences between Burgundy's greatest domaines — and applying this to blind tasting identification
lessons.6.slides.1.title: The Spectrum of Winemaking Philosophy
lessons.6.slides.1.content: The great Burgundy producers do not share a single philosophy — they span a spectrum from ultra-minimalist biodynamic (Leroy) to traditionally classic (Rousseau) to technically precise (Coche-Dury for whites). Understanding where each falls on this spectrum is the key to identifying their wines blind.
lessons.6.slides.2.title: 🔬 Key Winemaking Parameter Comparison
lessons.6.slides.2.points.0: Whole-cluster %: Dujac 70–100%, Rousseau 10–30%, Méo-Camuzet 30–50%, DRC 100%, Leroy 50–70%
lessons.6.slides.2.points.1: New oak %: DRC 100%, Leroy 0%, Rousseau 30–50%, Coche-Dury 15–30%, Méo-Camuzet 50–100%
lessons.6.slides.2.points.2: Yields: Leroy 10–15 hl/ha, DRC 20–25, Rousseau 28–32, Méo-Camuzet 30–35
lessons.6.slides.2.points.3: Farming: Leroy biodynamic, DRC biodynamic, Rousseau organic, Coche-Dury organic, others HVE
lessons.6.slides.3.title: Blind Tasting Identification: Whole-Cluster vs Destemmed
lessons.6.slides.3.leftPoints.0: Stems give 'green herb' or 'forest floor' notes at young age
lessons.6.slides.3.leftPoints.1: Redder fruit character (vs darker fruit in destemmed)
lessons.6.slides.3.leftPoints.3: More tannin from stems at first; then silkier over time
lessons.6.slides.3.rightPoints.2: Tannins softer earlier; from skin, not stems
lessons.6.slides.3.rightPoints.3: Lower apparent acidity at young age
lessons.6.slides.4.title: 👁️ Advanced Blind Tasting Identification Points
lessons.6.slides.4.points.0: DRC: supreme purity and precision; flowers AND earth; multi-dimensional; 'impossibly light'
lessons.6.slides.4.points.1: Leroy: extraordinary concentration with freshness; reductive at first; massive structure hiding behind elegance
lessons.6.slides.4.points.2: Rousseau: iron minerality; dark fruit; firm but noble tannin; very 'Gevrey'
lessons.6.slides.4.points.3: Dujac: high-toned red fruit; slight stem spice; transparent; 'singing' quality
lessons.6.slides.4.points.4: Méo-Camuzet: richness and structure; Vosne power; new oak evident but not dominant
lessons.6.slides.5.title: Traditional vs Modern Producers
lessons.6.slides.5.leftPoints.4: Examples: Rousseau, Vogüé, traditional Gevrey houses
lessons.6.slides.6.title: There Is No Single 'Best'
lessons.6.slides.6.content: One of the most important lessons in advanced Burgundy study: there is no objectively superior winemaking approach. DRC uses 100% whole clusters AND 100% new oak — a combination that defies convention yet produces sublime wine. Leroy uses no new oak and ultra-low yields — an equally distinct path to greatness. The 'correct' philosophy is the one that best expresses the specific terroir and vintage with which the producer works.
lessons.6.slides.7.title: 💡 Study Recommendations
lessons.6.slides.7.points.0: Taste across producers in the same appellation to isolate producer style from terroir
lessons.6.slides.7.points.1: Compare: Dujac Clos de la Roche vs Ponsot Clos de la Roche (same Grand Cru, very different styles)
lessons.6.slides.7.points.2: Compare: Rousseau Chambertin vs Trapet Chambertin (same Grand Cru, traditional vs biodynamic)
lessons.6.slides.7.points.3: Read producer interview collections: Clive Coates 'Côte d'Or', Matthew Croser 'Domaine profiles'
lessons.6.slides.7.points.4: Visit during harvest if possible — seeing the decisions made in real time is irreplaceable
